<Rep. Rosa L. DeLauro, Rep. Betty McCollum>: Pursuant to the provisions of clause 3(a)(1) of rule XIII of the Rules of the House of Representatives and section 6(i) of the Committee Rules, the views of the minority party of the House of Representatives, are printed below:
The Fiscal Year 2027 Defense Appropriations Bill totals $1.072 trillion. The Administration's total request for both mandatory and discretionary levels $1.5 trillion for the coming fiscal year for defense. This sum is an unprecedented topline request.
Broken out, this is a base budget increase of over $200 billion above last year's enacted level; mandatory funding is requested at $350 billion. The request is nearly a 44% increase in defense spending over last year.
This massive increase for defense comes as the President also proposes to cut domestic investments in the non-defense budget by $73 billion, or 10%. We know that cuts to other appropriations bills will deeply impact our national security-- particularly cuts to education and diplomacy.
In addition to the immense cuts to non-defense programs, we continue to have concerns about the Administration's split between discretionary funding that we control, and mandatory funding that we do not.
The Administration's reconciliation request includes many of their priorities such as Golden Dome, Drone Dominance, munitions and defense industrial base support. As of today, there is no guarantee it will pass. And if it does not, it will be nearly impossible to fix all the ``broken glass'' in a conferenced bill. The Administration must forego this approach in the fiscal year 2028 process.
In addition to the $1 trillion provided in fiscal year 2026 and the $1.5 trillion requested in Fiscal year 2027, the Administration is now requesting an additional $67 billion for the President's war with Iran. As of the writing of this document, the Committee is still waiting for the details of what this request encompasses. What the President said would be a six week conflict has evolved into a four month mess.
Our brave men and women in the military have won this war tactically, however, the strategic costs to our nation have been immense. The question must be answered at the end of this crisis--what will we have accomplished and at what cost?
Unfortunately, yet again, the bill did not include additional military support funding for Ukraine. The hostilities between Russia and Ukraine have now lasted longer than World War I--more than 1500 days. Every enacted Defense bill for the past eleven years has included funding for Ukraine and there remains broad Congressional support for the funding these programs. Therefore, we believe funding should be included. We look forward to working through the process to ensure funding continues.
It was disappointing that an amendment to follow the language in Fiscal Year 2026 National Defense Authorization Act (P.L. 119-60) for troop levels in European Command (EUCOM) failed in committee. The Administration's recent announcement of a six-month review of our personnel in NATO countries causes concern for many members, especially given the Administration's rash decisions over the past six months on troop levels and exercises in the EUCOM area of operations. Any additional removal of personnel and assets from EUCOM is exactly what Putin is hoping that the United States will do.
The bill now will include support for changing the name of the Department of Defense to the Department of War. This cosmetic alteration could cost up to $125 million to cover the costs of the necessary changes. When Congress and the Truman Administration reorganized our national security agencies in 1947, they made the decision to create the Department of Defense--and bring all the military services underneath it. The reason they chose ``defense'' instead of ``war'' was because they did not want to be overtly aggressive towards the Soviet Union. We should heed their wise decision. War is something we should want to avoid.
Finally, we were optimistic that going into the full committee markup the bill included only one poison pill provision. Unfortunately, an amendment to restore anti-LGBTQ, anti-DEI, anti-CRT and restrictions on reproductive health provisions were added to the bill in a party-line vote. Partisan riders bog down the appropriations process. They only extend deliberations until they are finally removed.
It should also be noted that none of these provisions are necessary under the current Administration. The Department of Defense does not conduct research on fetal tissue from abortions; does not have DEI programs; does not teach critical race and does not provide for the reproductive health needs of service members to the fullest extent necessary. Yet the attacks against equality for women, the LGBTQI community and diversity continue.
We are consistently concerned about what effect these provisions could have on recruitment and retention of military personnel. Any person, if they have the desire to serve, should have the opportunity to enlist in the U.S. Armed Forces. This bill should be laser focused on serving our warfighters and their families; that they have the equipment, training and support they need to execute their missions. It should not be focused on issues that divide us.
We have the most powerful military in the history of humankind. We are extraordinarily grateful to the men and women of our armed services who sacrifice everything to keep us safe. Their devotion to duty is exemplary, and it must be matched by the seriousness and sobriety of those at the very top of the chain of command.
For all of these reasons, we cannot yet support the bill as it is currently drafted. We look forward to working with the majority through the process of crafting a law that we all can support.
Rosa DeLauro.
Betty McCollum.
